newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - June 26.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - June 26.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories Thursday:
* The Dow Jones Industrials fell 68.08 points, resting at 7689.98 in a day marked by wide mood swings.
* A national commission has recommended that an independent panel be appointed to oversee the Internal Revenue Service and has suggested that the United States' tax code be simplified.
* U.S. President Bill Clinton has unveiled tough new controls on soot and smog.
* The U.S. Supreme Court rejected a settlement between asbestos manufactures and about 100,000 people claiming injuries from the substance.
* The U.S. Supreme Court upheld a federal program that requires agricultural companies to chip in for an industrywide advertising campaign.
* Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Discover & Co posted second quarter earnings that were up 3.9 percent over the prior year's second quarter.

* Public health advocates have objected to a key part of the proposed tobacco settlement, contending that any constraints on the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's authority to regulate nicotine are "absolutely unacceptable."
* Thailand Finance Minister Thanong Bidya has moved to repair the country's financial system, but analysts are skeptical the government has the resolve to rejuvenate its faltering economy.
* A group of movie producers has formed the Producers Credit Board to lobby studios to be careful in doling out credits, which some producers believe are too frequent for work that is not deserving.
* McKay Nursery Co has evolved into an employee-owned enterprise that offers seasonal workers a stock plan that makes them feel as though they have a stake in improving operations.
* South Africans will soon be allowed for the first time in more than three decades to own assets overseas, a move that will have uncertain results.
* The U.S. Justice Department has urged telephone regulators to reject a bid by Ameritech Corp to offer long-distance service in Michigan.

* The U.S. Supreme Court has upheld the Securities and Exchange Commission's contention that insider trading laws apply to people who have confidential information even if they have no connection to the company whose shares are being purchased.
